div.div: Fully managed ML service to build, train, and deploy ML models
Can use Mechanical Turk as its human workforce source
Unlike Mechanical Turk, it includes ML automation to skip obvious cases and reduce cost
Ground Truth — builds high-quality training datasets; automated + human labeling
Ground Truth Plus — fully managed data labeling service; AWS manages the labeling workforce so you don't need to set up your own pipeline
Feature Store — fully managed repository to store, share, and manage ML features
JumpStart — ML hub to evaluate, compare, and select Foundation Models quickly
Canvas — no-code interface to create ML models
Clarify — explains how ML models make predictions (model explainability)
Data Wrangler — simplifies data preparation and feature engineering
Model Monitor — monitors ML models in production; detects data drift, model quality drift, and accuracy drift
Model Cards — documentation for ML models (governance and reporting)
Model Dashboard — centralized view aggregating Model Cards, Model Monitor, and endpoint metrics in one place
Inference Endpoint — allows clients to invoke deployed models and receive predictions
Autopilot — automatically trains, tunes, and selects the best ML model for your data (AutoML); no ML expertise required
Role Manager — simplifies creating IAM roles for ML personas (data scientist, MLOps engineer, etc.)
Unified Studio — collaborative workspace for teams working on data and AI projects together
MLflow integration — track, organize, view, analyze, and compare ML experiments
AI Service Cards — documents intended use cases, limitations, and responsible AI design choices

Rekognition — image and video analysis; supports object detection, facial analysis, content moderation, and celebrity recognition; image/video only — does NOT support multilingual text experiences or language-based tasks
Comprehend Medical — extracts medical information (conditions, medications, dosages) from clinical text
Comprehend — derives insights from text within documents
Transcribe Medical — speech-to-text specialized for medical terminology and clinical documentation
Transcribe — converts speech/audio to text
Polly — converts text to speech in dozens of languages
Textract — extracts text, handwriting, layout elements, and data from scanned documents (OCR)
Lex — builds conversational interfaces (chatbots) using voice and text; powers Alexa
Personalize — generates product and content recommendations
Forecast — highly accurate time-series forecasts using statistical and ML algorithms
Does NOT detect accuracy/data drift — that is SageMaker Model Monitor's job
Augmented AI (A2I) — human review workflows for ML predictions; routes low-confidence predictions to humans
Kendra — enterprise search service powered by ML (searches manuals, reports, FAQs, HR docs)
Trainium — ML chip purpose-built for deep learning training of 100B+ parameter models; more energy-efficient than equivalent GPU-based training; lower cost and carbon footprint
Inferentia — ML chip for high-performance inference at low cost
DeepRacer — autonomous 1/18th scale Wi-Fi enabled physical race car that drives itself on a physical track; used to test and learn reinforcement learning models in a real-world environment
ML Tools
Fully managed service to build and scale Gen AI applications using foundation models
Higher → more diverse and creative responses (more candidates in the pool)
Lower → more focused and deterministic responses (fewer candidates)
Top-K — number of most likely candidates the model considers for the next token
Higher → larger pool of tokens; more varied and unpredictable output
Lower → only the most probable tokens; more conservative and consistent output
Top-P — percentage of most likely candidates the model considers for the next token
Higher → more creative and unpredictable responses
Lower → more deterministic and repetitive responses
Temperature — controls randomness of the model's responses
Present → generation halts immediately when sequence is encountered
Absent → model generates until max token limit is reached
Stop sequences — character sequences that stop the model from generating further tokens
Response length — sets the minimum and maximum number of tokens the model generates in a response
Inference Parameters
On-Demand — pay as you go; does NOT support model customization (no fine-tuning)
Provisioned Throughput — reserves capacity in advance; REQUIRED for fine-tuned or customized models; supports continued pre-training
Batch Inference — processes large numbers of requests asynchronously; lowest cost per request
Inference Modes
Continued Pre-training — uses UNLABELED data; makes models more domain-specific
Fine-tuning — uses LABELED data; improves performance on specific tasks
Domain Adaptation Fine-Tuning — a form of fine-tuning that uses domain-specific labeled data to adapt a general model to a specialized field (e.g. legal, medical)
Model Customization
Playground — console environment to experiment with models; no fine-tuning support
Model Evaluation — prepares data, trains models, selects metrics, tests, analyzes, and monitors
Agents — complete complex tasks for generative AI applications
Responses include citations back to source documents, so users can verify answers
Improves user confidence — knowing responses are backed by real source documents makes users more willing to act on the answers
Reduces hallucination by grounding the model in real documents rather than memory
Knowledge Bases (RAG) — gives FMs contextual information from private data sources for RAG
Guardrails — detects sensitive information such as PII in prompts or model responses
Watermark Detection — identifies images generated by Amazon Titan Image Generator
PartyRock — individual Gen AI app playground for experimentation (not for team collaboration)
Generative AI-powered assistant family; each variant targets a specific domain
Q Developer — assists developers and IT professionals with coding, testing, security scanning, and AWS resource optimization
Q Business — fully managed generative AI assistant for enterprise data (IT, HR, help desks); uses IAM Identity Center for user authentication and access management
Success metrics: Average Call Duration (shorter = faster resolution), First Contact Resolution rate, Customer Satisfaction (CSAT)
Q in Connect — contact center service; recommends responses and actions for customer service agents
Q in QuickSight — generative BI assistant; builds dashboards and visualizations from natural language
Gen AI Tools
records AWS API calls and delivers log files for auditing
assesses, audits, and evaluates the configurations of AWS resources
continuously audits AWS usage for risk and compliance
provides guidance to provision resources following AWS best practices
automated vulnerability management; scans workloads for software vulnerabilities
on-demand access to AWS compliance reports and online agreements
vector store used for Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock
cloud-native BI service for creating dashboards and visualizations from data sources; integrates with ML insights
cloud-based contact center service; powers customer service operations; integrates with Q in Connect for AI-assisted responses
private connection between a VPC and AWS services (e.g. S3, SageMaker) without traffic going over the public internet; required for compliance scenarios where data must not leave the AWS network
serverless event bus; routes events between AWS services and applications; used to trigger workflows from model invocations or audit events
Other AWS Services
Tools
Artificial Intelligence → Machine Learning → Deep Learning → Generative AI
Artificial Intelligence — broad field of making machines simulate human intelligence
Machine Learning — subset of AI; learns patterns from data without being explicitly programmed
Deep Learning — subset of ML; uses multi-layered neural networks to learn complex patterns from large amounts of data
Generative AI — subset of deep learning; models that can generate new content (text, images, audio, code) rather than just classifying or predicting
Layers of interconnected nodes (neurons); each layer learns increasingly abstract features
Weights — numerical parameters adjusted during training to improve predictions
Gradient Descent — optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts weights by moving in the direction that reduces the loss (error); the core mechanism of neural network training
Backpropagation — calculates how much each weight contributed to the error, then uses gradient descent to update all weights simultaneously
Example: spam email detection — each email is labeled spam or not spam
Supervised — trains on labeled data to predict specific outputs
Example: customer segmentation — grouping customers by purchase behavior with no predefined labels
Unsupervised — trains on unlabeled data; spots patterns and categorizes data (clustering, dimensionality reduction)
Example: fraud detection — few labeled fraud cases combined with many unlabeled transactions
Semi-supervised — combines supervised and unsupervised techniques
Example: GPT pre-training — model predicts the next word from raw text, no human labels needed
Self-supervised — model generates its own labels from vast amounts of raw/unlabeled data
Example: DeepRacer learns to stay on track by receiving rewards for correct driving decisions
Reinforcement — model learns through trial and error by receiving rewards for correct actions
Example: ChatGPT fine-tuning — human raters preferred more helpful responses, shaping model behavior
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) — humans rate model outputs; ratings are used to train a reward model that guides further fine-tuning
Example: ImageNet-trained image model fine-tuned to classify medical X-rays
Transfer Learning — pre-trained model adapted to a different but related task
Example: recommendation system that continuously adapts to new user preferences
Incremental Learning — model adapts to new data over time without forgetting previous knowledge
Example: image classification, object detection, medical imaging analysis
CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) — specialized for image and spatial data; uses convolutional layers to detect patterns like edges, shapes, and textures
Example: high-accuracy image recognition tasks where shallow networks underfit
ResNet (Residual Network) — deep CNN variant that uses skip connections to prevent vanishing gradients; enables training very deep networks (50–200+ layers)
Example: video understanding — processes each frame while carrying context from prior frames; predicting next word in a sentence
RNN (Recurrent Neural Network) — processes sequential data by maintaining a hidden state across time steps; suited for time-series, speech, and video
Use when: interpretability is required and model must be explainable to non-technical stakeholders
Example: explaining why a loan was approved or denied — each branch shows the exact rule applied
Decision Trees — interpretable model that splits data on feature thresholds into a tree of decisions; easy for humans to read and explain
TP — model predicted positive, was actually positive ✓ (e.g. spam email correctly caught)
TN — model predicted negative, was actually negative ✓ (e.g. normal email correctly passed)
FP — model predicted positive, was actually negative ✗ (false alarm — e.g. normal email blocked)
FN — model predicted negative, was actually positive ✗ (missed — e.g. spam email lands in inbox)
Use when: you need detailed breakdown of a classification model's errors
Example: email spam filter — how many spam/legitimate emails were correctly or incorrectly classified
Confusion Matrix — displays True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP), False Negatives (FN)
Use when: understanding relationships between features before model training
Example: house price prediction — checking whether size, location, and age are correlated before training
Correlation Matrix — measures statistical correlation between variables
Use when: large prediction errors are especially costly (sensitive to outliers)
Example: electricity demand forecasting for a power grid — one huge error (off by 500MW) could cause a blackout, so large errors must be punished heavily
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) — average error in regression models; penalizes large errors more
Use when: all errors are equally important; more robust to outliers than RMSE
Example: daily temperature forecasting — being off by 4°C is exactly twice as bad as being off by 2°C, no more, no less
MAE (Mean Absolute Error) — average magnitude of errors in predictions
Example: spam filter — you want every flagged email to truly be spam, not block legitimate mail
Precision — of all predicted positives, how many were actually positive; use when false positives are costly
Example: cancer screening — you want to catch every real case, even at the cost of some false alarms
Recall — of all actual positives, how many were correctly predicted; use when false negatives are costly
Use when: assessing quality of machine-generated translations
Example: evaluating Google Translate output against a professional human translator's version
BLEU Score — absolute metric (0–1 scale); evaluates machine translation quality by n-gram overlap with reference translations
Use when: assessing quality of automatic text summarization
Example: evaluating an AI-generated news article summary against a human-written summary
ROUGE — evaluates text summarization by n-gram overlap with reference summaries
Use when: meaning matters more than exact word match (paraphrase, semantic equivalence)
Example: "the car is fast" and "the vehicle is quick" should score high despite having no words in common
BERT Score — evaluates semantic similarity between generated and reference text using contextual embeddings
Use when: classes are balanced; simple binary or multi-class classification
Example: cat vs. dog image classifier with equal numbers of cat and dog training images
Accuracy — ratio of correct predictions over total predictions
Use when: classes are imbalanced; both false positives and false negatives matter equally
Example: rare disease diagnosis — missing a sick patient (FN) is as costly as a false alarm (FP)
F1 Score — harmonic mean of Precision and Recall; balances both metrics
Use when: automated metrics cannot capture nuance (e.g. tone, cultural sensitivity, factual correctness)
Human Evaluation — human judges rate model outputs for quality, relevance, or safety; more accurate but slower and costlier than automated metrics
Example: "Why was this specific loan application rejected?" — shows how income, credit score, and age each contributed to that one decision
Shapley Values — local method; explains individual predictions; impact per feature per instance
Example: "How does income level generally affect loan approval across all applicants?" — shows the overall trend, not any single case
Partial Dependence Plots (PDP) — global method; overall relationship between a feature and model output
Example: fraud detection at checkout — must respond in milliseconds before the transaction completes
Real-time — low latency; responses needed immediately; high cost
Example: genomics analysis or document processing — large payload, no immediate response needed
Asynchronous — queues requests; handles in background; supports large payloads up to 1 GB; use for long-running jobs (up to 1 hour)
Example: nightly sales forecasting across millions of records
Batch — processes large datasets all at once; handles larger payloads (several GBs+)
Example: occasional image moderation app — idle most of the time, spikes unpredictably
Serverless — scales automatically; best for unpredictable or sporadic traffic
Epochs — one complete pass through the entire training dataset; more epochs = more learning but risk of overfitting
Hyperparameters — control the training process (e.g. learning rate, number of epochs, batch size); set before training; prevent overfitting
Model Parameters — define a model's behavior in interpreting input and generating responses
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) — examines data via statistics and visualizations to identify patterns and anomalies
Cross-validation — splits data into k folds; trains on k-1, tests on the remaining fold, rotates; gives reliable estimate of generalization without wasting data
Structured Data — organized in rows and columns (databases, spreadsheets); easy to query and process
Unstructured Data — no predefined format (text, images, audio, video); requires ML to extract meaning
Example: PCA compresses 100 features down to 10 principal components that explain 95% of variance
Dimensionality Reduction — reduces the number of input features while retaining the most important information; improves training speed and reduces overfitting
Feature Selection — choosing which existing features to keep or discard based on relevance; no transformation, just filtering
Feature Extraction — transforming raw data into new derived features (e.g. embeddings, PCA components); creates new representations
Example: grouping customers into segments based on purchase behaviour
K-Means — unsupervised clustering algorithm; assigns data points to k clusters based on similarity; no labels needed
Example: recommending a product by finding the k most similar users who bought it
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) — supervised classification algorithm; classifies a point by majority vote of its k nearest neighbours in feature space
Data Lineage — tracks the origin, transformations, and movement of data through a pipeline; critical for compliance, debugging, and reproducibility
Synthetic Data — artificially generated data that mimics real data distributions; used when real data is scarce, sensitive, or imbalanced
Labeled Data — data with annotations or ground-truth answers; required for supervised learning
Unlabeled Data — raw data with no annotations; used in unsupervised and self-supervised learning
Multi-class Classification — each input belongs to exactly one class out of many (e.g. digit recognition: 0–9)
Multi-label Classification — each input can belong to multiple classes simultaneously (e.g. a news article tagged as both "sports" and "finance")
Example: detecting pedestrians, cars, and traffic signs simultaneously in a single camera frame
Object Detection — computer vision task that identifies and locates multiple objects within an image with bounding boxes; contrast with image classification which only labels the whole image
Computer Vision — field of AI that enables machines to interpret and understand visual information (images, video); output is understanding/meaning (e.g. "this is a cat")
Key distinction: Computer Vision = understanding images; Image Processing = transforming images
Image Processing — manipulation and enhancement of images using algorithms; output is a transformed image, not interpretation (e.g. sharpening, noise removal, resizing)
Example: model trained on outdated customer data predicts wrong product preferences
Data Quality — missing values, inconsistent entries, noise, insufficient dataset size
Example: a student who memorizes past exam questions word-for-word but fails when the wording changes slightly
Overfitting — model learns training data too well including noise; performs great on training data but poorly on new data
Example: a student who only studies one topic and guesses everything else — too little learning to generalize
Underfitting — model is too simple to learn the underlying pattern; performs poorly on both training and new data
Fix: data augmentation, oversampling (SMOTE), undersampling, class-weighted loss functions
Example: fraud detection — 99.9% of transactions are legitimate, so model predicts "not fraud" for everything
Class Imbalance — one class has far more samples than another; model learns to always predict the majority class
Example: hiring model trained on historical data that unfairly favors certain demographics
Sampling Bias — training data does not represent the full population
Measurement Bias — systematic error in how data is recorded or collected
Observer Bias — human labelers introduce their own perspectives into annotations
Confirmation Bias — model or analyst interprets results to confirm existing beliefs
Bias — imbalanced data causes model to favor majority class; can perpetuate discrimination
Example: a bank can't explain why its deep learning model denied a loan — creates a regulatory problem
Model Explainability — complex models are hard to interpret; affects trust and ethics
Example: training a large language model requires weeks across hundreds of GPUs
Scalability — large datasets require significant compute; AWS cloud services help
ML Concepts
Use when: need a general-purpose base to fine-tune for a specific domain
Foundation Models — trained on massive datasets; broad base; use self-supervised learning
Use when: task involves text — chat, summarization, translation, Q&A, code generation
Large Language Models (LLM) — class of Foundation Models specialized for understanding and generating human language
Use when: resource-constrained environments, edge devices, or single-domain use cases where a full LLM is overkill
Small Language Models (SLM) — lightweight language models optimized for specific, narrow tasks; lower cost and latency than LLMs
Example: a model that takes an image + a text question and returns a text answer (visual Q&A)
Multimodal Models — accept and/or generate multiple data types (text, image, audio, video) within a single model
Contrast: Generative Models learn the full data distribution to create new samples; Discriminative Models only classify
Discriminative Models — learn the boundary between classes; predict a label or output from input features
Use when: high-quality image or audio generation from text prompts (e.g. Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, Midjourney)
Diffusion Models — gradually destroys a real image by adding noise, then trains to reverse the process; generates new content by denoising random static step by step
Use when: creating deepfakes, synthetic training data, or realistic face/image generation
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) — two competing networks: generator creates fakes, discriminator judges real vs fake; they push each other until fakes are indistinguishable from real
Use when: data compression, anomaly detection, or generating variations of existing data
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) — encoder compresses input into a compact representation; decoder reconstructs data from it
Token — unit of text (word or subword) the model processes; fewer tokens = lower cost
Context Window — amount of text (in tokens) the model can consider at once
Embeddings — vector representations encoding semantic meaning of words or phrases
BERT — bidirectional Transformer; reads text in both directions; strong at understanding context; used for classification, Q&A, and semantic search
GPT — autoregressive Transformer; generates text left-to-right; strong at text generation, code, and conversation
Transformer Models — neural network for sequential data; uses self-attention + contextual embeddings
Non-determinism — same prompt can produce different outputs on each run; caused by temperature and sampling randomness; intentional design for creativity
Optimizes LLM output by referencing an external knowledge base before generating a response
Extends LLM capabilities to specific domains without retraining the model
Cost-effective; keeps responses relevant, accurate, and useful

RAG vs. Agents — RAG retrieves documents and augments the prompt; Agents take multi-step actions (call APIs, run code, chain decisions) — use Agents when the task requires planning and tool use, not just retrieval
1. Prompt Engineering — lowest cost; no training; adjust how you ask the model
2. RAG — moderate cost; no model changes; inject fresh external knowledge at query time
3. Fine-tuning — higher cost; retrains model on labeled data; improves task-specific behaviour
4. Continued Pre-training — highest cost; retrains on large unlabeled corpus; deepest domain adaptation
Performance Improvement Order (increasing cost/effort, increasing performance gain)
Prompt Structure — a well-formed prompt typically contains: Instructions (what to do), Context (background info), Input Data (the content to act on), Output Indicator (desired format or answer type)
Zero-shot — presents a task to the model without any examples
Few-shot — provides a few examples to guide the model's output
Negative Prompting — guides the model to avoid certain outputs or behaviors
Chain-of-thought — breaks complex questions into smaller logical steps; enhances reasoning
Example: injecting a user's purchase history into the prompt to personalize product recommendations
Dynamic Prompting — customizes prompt content at runtime based on user attributes, context, or retrieved data
Prompt Optimization — iteratively testing and adjusting prompts to improve output consistency and accuracy
Gen AI Concepts
Concepts
Fairness — models treat all individuals and groups equitably; avoid outputs that discriminate
Transparency — ability to understand and explain how AI systems make decisions and what data they use
Privacy & Security — protecting data used to train and query AI models; preventing unauthorized access or leakage
Explainability — providing human-understandable reasons for model outputs; supports trust and accountability
Accountability — clear ownership and oversight of AI systems and their outcomes; audit trails
Safety — preventing harm; ensuring AI behaves within intended boundaries and does not produce dangerous outputs
Governance — policies, processes, and auditing frameworks to manage AI responsibly across an organization
Robustness — model performs reliably across diverse inputs, edge cases, and adversarial conditions
Controllability — ability to adjust, correct, retrain, or shut down AI systems when behavior is unacceptable
AWS Dimensions
Hallucination — model generates plausible-sounding but false or unsupported responses
Toxicity — AI-generated content that is offensive, disturbing, or inappropriate
Plagiarism — presenting someone else's work without proper attribution
Bias — content that unfairly favors or discriminates against certain groups
Misinterpretation — meaning or intent of text is misunderstood or conveyed incorrectly
Poisoning — intentional introduction of malicious/biased data into the training dataset
Prompt Leaking — unintentional disclosure of prompts/inputs, exposing protected data
Jailbreaking — crafting inputs that trick the model into ignoring its safety guidelines and producing harmful or restricted content
Prompt Injection — embedding malicious instructions inside user input or retrieved documents to override the model's intended behaviour
Prompt Hijacking — redirecting the model away from its intended task by injecting conflicting instructions (a form of prompt injection)
Risks & Failure Modes
AI Governance — ethical guidelines, auditing processes, and accountability frameworks for AI systems across the organization
Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix — defines security ownership across layers: data, model, infrastructure, and application
Shared Responsibility Model — AWS secures the infrastructure (security OF the cloud); customers secure their data, access controls, and model behavior (security IN the cloud)
Bedrock Service Role — IAM role granted to Amazon Bedrock so it can access S3, KMS, and other resources on your behalf; scope the role per team/project to enforce least-privilege data access
Data Residency — where data is physically stored; compliance regulations may require data to remain in specific geographic locations
Data Retention — how long data is kept before deletion; governed by policy or regulation
Threat Detection — identifying active, ongoing attacks or suspicious activity (e.g. GuardDuty)
Vulnerability Management — proactively finding and fixing weaknesses before they are exploited (e.g. Inspector)
Governance & Security
Responsible AI
each AWS Region consists of a minimum of 3 Availability Zones
each AZ consists of one or more discrete data centers
Regional — deployed and scoped to a specific region (e.g. SageMaker, Bedrock, EC2, S3)
Global — operate across all regions from a single configuration (e.g. IAM, CloudFront, Route 53)
Infrastructure
access to networking, compute, and storage; highest flexibility (e.g., EC2)
removes need to manage underlying infrastructure (e.g., Elastic Beanstalk)
complete product run and managed by the service provider (e.g., S3, Rekognition)
combines on-premises infrastructure with cloud services; data stays on-premises for compliance while cloud handles scale and compute
Service Models
pay only for what you use; no upfront investment in servers or data centers

div.strong: Trade fixed expense for variable expense

div.div: AWS buys hardware in bulk so unit costs are lower than running your own infrastructure

div.strong: Benefit from massive economies of scale

div.div: scale up or down on demand; no risk of over-provisioning (wasted money) or under-provisioning (poor performance)
new resources available in minutes instead of weeks
focus budget on your product, not on physical infrastructure

div.strong: Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers

div.div: deploy to any AWS Region worldwide with just a few clicks
Cloud Benefits (6 Advantages)
pay as you go; no upfront commitment
reserves capacity in advance for a discounted rate
cost savings with risk of interruptions (EC2 only, not Bedrock)
one- or three-year commitment (EC2 only, not Bedrock)
